chapters.name: Types of Life Policies and Annuities
chapters.summary: Whole life, limited-pay and single-premium life, universal, variable and indexed life, the kinds of term insurance, joint and survivorship plans, and annuities from the accumulation period to the payout options.
keyPoints: Ordinary (straight) whole life: level premium paid to age 100 or 121; cash value equals the face amount at maturity.
Limited-pay life: premiums stop after a set number of years or at a set age, but coverage lasts for the whole of life.
Universal life has two parts: a death benefit and a cash account; Option A pays a level benefit, Option B pays the face plus the cash value.
Variable life puts cash value in separate accounts; the policyholder carries the investment risk, and the seller needs a securities license too.
Decreasing term fits a debt that shrinks, such as a mortgage; level term keeps the same face amount for the whole term.
Joint life pays at the first death; survivorship (second-to-die) life pays at the second death.
Annuity: accumulation period = paying in; annuity (payout) period = receiving payments; the annuitant's life is the measuring life.

chapters.name: Life Policy Riders, Provisions, and Options
chapters.summary: Riders that add benefits, the standard provisions in every life policy, beneficiary designations, premium payment rules, nonforfeiture and dividend options, settlement options, and common exclusions.
keyPoints: Waiver of premium usually needs a waiting period of about 6 months of total disability before premiums are waived.
Guaranteed insurability lets the insured buy more coverage at set ages or events without proof of insurability.
Grace period for life premiums is usually 30 or 31 days; coverage stays in force, and a death in that time is paid minus the unpaid premium.
Incontestability: after the policy has been in force 2 years, the insurer cannot void it for misstatements on the application (fraud rules vary by state).
Nonforfeiture options: cash surrender, reduced paid-up (lower face, no more premiums, for life), extended term (same face, for a limited time).
Misstatement of age or gender: the benefit is adjusted to what the premium paid would have bought at the correct age or gender.
Irrevocable beneficiary must agree before the owner changes the beneficiary or takes a policy loan.

chapters.name: Life Application, Underwriting, and Delivery
chapters.summary: Completing and signing the application, representations and warranties, replacement, privacy and anti-money-laundering rules, insurable interest, medical information and consumer reports, risk classes, policy delivery, and the legal features of an insurance contract.
keyPoints: The application is signed by the proposed insured, the policyowner (if different), and the agent.
Insurable interest must exist when the life policy is issued; it does not need to exist at the time of death.
Statements on an application are representations (true to the best of knowledge); warranties must be literally true.
Conditional receipt: coverage starts on the application date (or medical exam date, if later) if the applicant is insurable as applied for.
Risk classes: preferred, standard, substandard (rated), and declined.
Insurance contract features: aleatory (unequal exchange), adhesion (insurer writes it), unilateral (only the insurer promises), conditional.
Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, an applicant must be told when a consumer report is ordered and who supplied it if coverage is declined or rated.

chapters.name: Retirement Plans, Taxes, and Other Life Concepts
chapters.summary: Third-party ownership, life settlements, group life and its conversion privilege, qualified and nonqualified retirement plans, needs analysis for families and businesses, Social Security survivor benefits, and the tax treatment of premiums, proceeds, dividends, and modified endowment contracts.
keyPoints: Life insurance death proceeds paid as a lump sum to a named beneficiary are generally free of federal income tax.
Premiums for individual life insurance are not tax-deductible for a person.
Dividends are a return of excess premium and are not taxable until they exceed the total premiums paid.
Group life conversion: a leaving employee usually has 31 days to convert to an individual permanent policy without proof of insurability.
Qualified plans: employer contributions are deductible and growth is tax-deferred; nonqualified plans may favor key employees.
A policy that fails the 7-pay test becomes a modified endowment contract (MEC); loans and withdrawals are taxed gains first, plus a 10% penalty before age 59½.
Key person insurance: the business owns, pays, and is the beneficiary.

chapters.name: Types of Health Policies
chapters.summary: Disability income and business disability policies, accidental death and dismemberment, medical expense plans from basic and major medical to HMO, PPO and POS, HSAs, FSAs and HRAs, Medicare supplement, group coverage and COBRA, long-term care, and limited policies such as dental, cancer, and hospital indemnity.
keyPoints: Disability income replaces lost income; benefits are often limited to about 60% to 70% of earnings.
Business overhead expense pays office costs such as rent and staff salaries, not the owner's own income.
AD&D pays the principal sum for accidental death; dismemberment or loss of sight often pays a capital sum, a part of the principal sum.
HMO: a primary care physician acts as gatekeeper and care is mostly in-network; PPO: you can go out of network at higher cost.
An HSA must be paired with a high deductible health plan; the money belongs to the account holder and rolls over each year.
COBRA lets employees of employers with 20 or more workers keep group health coverage, usually 18 months after job loss, paying up to 102% of the premium.
Long-term care eligibility usually needs a cognitive impairment or inability to do 2 of the 6 activities of daily living.

chapters.name: Health Policy Provisions, Clauses, and Riders
chapters.summary: The mandatory and optional uniform provisions in individual health policies, including grace period, notice of claim, proof of loss, and time limit on certain defenses; other clauses such as probationary and elimination periods, deductibles and coinsurance; riders; and renewability types.
keyPoints: Grace period: 7 days for weekly premium, 10 days for monthly, 31 days for all other modes.
Notice of claim: within 20 days of the loss, or as soon as reasonably possible.
Claim forms: the insurer must send them within 15 days of the notice of claim.
Proof of loss: within 90 days of the loss; no later than 1 year unless the claimant lacks legal capacity.
Time limit on certain defenses: after 2 years the insurer cannot deny a claim for misstatements on the application, except fraud.
Legal actions: no lawsuit until 60 days after proof of loss, and none after 3 years.
Noncancelable: the insurer cannot cancel or raise premiums; guaranteed renewable: cannot cancel but can raise premiums for a whole class.

chapters.name: Medicare, Medicaid, and Social Security
chapters.summary: The four parts of Medicare, who qualifies, and what each part covers; Medicaid as a joint federal-state program for people with low income; and Social Security disability and survivor benefits.
keyPoints: Medicare Part A = hospital insurance; Part B = medical (doctor and outpatient) insurance; Part C = Medicare Advantage; Part D = prescription drugs.
Medicare covers people 65 and older, people who have received Social Security disability benefits for 24 months, and people with end-stage renal disease.
Medicare does not pay for long-term custodial care.
Medicaid is run by the states with federal and state money and is based on financial need.
Social Security disability needs a disability expected to last at least 12 months or end in death, and a 5-month waiting period.

chapters.name: Other Health Insurance Concepts
chapters.summary: Total, partial, residual, and recurrent disability; owner's rights and beneficiaries; dependent children; coordination of benefits; occupational and nonoccupational coverage; tax treatment of health and disability benefits; managed care; workers compensation; and subrogation.
keyPoints: Own occupation: unable to do your own job; any occupation: unable to do any job suited to your education and experience.
Residual disability pays a part of the benefit in proportion to the income lost while you work at a reduced level.
Disability benefits from an individual policy paid with after-tax money are tax-free; if the employer paid the premium, benefits are taxable.
Coordination of benefits: the primary plan pays first, and total payments from all plans cannot exceed 100% of the allowable expenses.
Subrogation: after paying a claim, the insurer takes over the insured's right to recover from the party who caused the loss.

chapters.name: Health Field Underwriting and Contract Law
chapters.summary: Completing the health application, sources of insurability information such as the MIB and consumer reports, HIPAA privacy, collecting the first premium and giving receipts, submitting the application, policy delivery, replacement, and contract law terms.
keyPoints: Collect the first premium with the application whenever possible and give the applicant a receipt.
The MIB (Medical Information Bureau) shares coded medical information among member insurers; it is not a reason by itself to decline coverage.
Errors on the application are corrected by drawing a line through, writing the correct answer, and having the applicant initial it; no correction fluid.
If the premium was not collected with the application, the agent gets a statement of good health when delivering the policy.
Replacement means a new policy will cause an existing one to lapse or be reduced; the agent must follow the state's replacement rules and notices.
